newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain employers stand firm before key labour talks.
newsitem.headline: Spain employers stand firm before key labour talks.

text.p: The Spanish employers' association CEOE said on Tuesday that it would not soften proposals, nor succumb to political pressure, to agree badly-needed labour reform with unions.
Just before final talks were due to begin, CEOE president Juan Maria Cuevas said the employers were not going to sign "just anything".
"We will assume all the costs that might go along with a disagreement, but we are convinced the deal must be effective," he told a news conference.

Spanish unions and employers have been negotiating this year for ways to reform a rigid labour market that suffers from more than 20 percent unemployment -- more than double the European Union average.
The conservative Popular Party has vowed to step in and impose new regulations if the two fail to reach an accord.
But Cuevas said employers did not plan to revamp their offer, which has been on the table since December.
He added that it would take a "maximum effort" in the final talks to bring employers and trade unions together.
"We still don't know how to reach a deal on some dismissals," Cuevas said.
An official with the General Workers' Union (UGT), one of Spain's two biggest, was equally adamant that the current employer posture was inadequate.

"It is perfectly understandable why unions reject this," UGT Secretary for Union Action Toni Ferrer told Spanish national radio. "Because it would be tantamount to destroying employment and the possibilities for stable employment in our country."
The main sticking point has been the high cost of dismissing workers, which has dissuaded employers from hiring permanent workers in favour of temporary workers with contracts for up to three years.
A Labour Ministry survey found that more than 96 percent of new jobs created in 1996 were temporary, and half of those were on contracts lasting less than a month.
Employers want to reduce dismissal costs for permanent workers, while unions are determined to solve the problem of contract instability that plagues Spain's labour market.
The two sides have reached a partial agreement on dismissal costs. Employers have accepted trade union demands that severance for unfair dismissal be maintained at 45 days.

The CEOE insists, however, that legitimate dismissal costs should be reduced to 20 days for each year worked with a maximum outlay of 12 months salary from the current situation which tends to favour the employee with typically higher payments.
